course_title: Cognitive Load Theory for Dashboard Design
discipline_framing: The science of working-memory limits applied to information design — managing intrinsic, extraneous, and germane load so complex dashboards inform users without overwhelming or fatiguing them
audience: Dashboard and BI designers, analytics-product teams, and visualization engineers who must fit dense, decision-critical information inside the narrow bottleneck of human working memory
sources: Sweller's cognitive load theory — the instructional-design foundation (intrinsic, extraneous, and germane load with the element-interactivity basis)
Baddeley's working-memory model (phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, central executive) and Cowan's revised capacity findings (the four-chunk limit)
Miller's magical number seven lineage with the chunking and recoding tradition
Mayer's multimedia learning principles (coherence, signaling, spatial-contiguity, temporal-contiguity, modality, redundancy) as the experimentally tested load-management toolkit
Paas-van Merrienboer load measurement tradition (subjective rating scales, task-performance triangulation) and NASA-TLX workload assessment
Stephen Few's dashboard design doctrine (glanceability, information density, chart-selection for monitoring) as the applied BI synthesis
Pirolli-Card information foraging theory for navigation-load and scent-following analysis
pitfalls: Treating load as only-about-quantity — element interactivity, not element count, drives intrinsic load: four interacting series can cost more than forty parallel ones
Optimizing extraneous load to zero while ignoring germane load — frictionless displays that teach nothing, leaving users permanently dependent on the designer's pre-chewing
Expertise-reversal blindness — scaffolding that helps novices (guides, annotations, step-by-step layering) becoming redundant load for experts, one design serving neither
Density panic — stripping legitimate information to reduce felt complexity, when the real fix is structure: chunking, alignment, and progressive disclosure carrying density at low load
Measuring load by asking designers — self-report from the display's authors is worthless; load evidence requires naive users, workload scales, and performance triangulation
